The card lists the two returned sets, 0 as A, C, E and 1 as B, D, F." width="100%"} A bipartite graph is one whose nodes split into two groups such that every edge joins a node in one group to a node in the other (no edge runs within a group). This method finds such a split by 2-coloring: it starts at a node, gives it color `0`, gives its neighbors color `1`, their neighbors color `0`, and so on. If two adjacent nodes ever end up with the same color, the graph has an odd cycle and is not bipartite. The numbering is deterministic: components are processed in ascending node-ID order, and in each connected component the side containing the component's lowest node ID goes into the first set. Isolated nodes therefore always land in the first set. In a disconnected graph each component is colored independently, so the split is only one of several valid ones. The sets are what the `which=` argument of `bipartite_projection()` and the bipartite centrality methods refer to. Bipartite structure shows up whenever a network links two kinds of entity, such as: - people and the groups, events, or projects they belong to - genes and diseases, or drugs and their targets - customers and products, or authors and papers Note that the coloring is discovered from the edges alone; node attributes like a `type` column are not consulted. Use `is_bipartite()` if you only need a yes/no answer. The whole graph is used and the current selection is ignored. On a directed graph edge direction is ignored: the partition is that of the underlying undirected graph, matching `is_bipartite()`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple[list[int], list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A pair `(set_0, set_1)` of sorted lists of node IDs. Every node appears in exactly one of the two lists. An empty graph returns `([], [])`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is not bipartite (it contains an odd-length cycle, such as a triangle, or a self-loop). ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A small gene-disease network splits into its genes and its diseases. Mapping the IDs back to labels shows which side each node landed on: ::: {#67fd0292 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["Gene1", "Gene2", "Disease1", "Disease2"]) .add_edges([("Gene1", "Disease1"), ("Gene1", "Disease2"), ("Gene2", "Disease1")]) ) set_a, set_b = graph.bipartite_sets() ( [graph.get_label_from_id(i) for i in set_a], [graph.get_label_from_id(i) for i in set_b], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (['Gene1', 'Gene2'], ['Disease1', 'Disease2']) ``` ::: ::: Isolated nodes and separate components are each colored on their own, starting from their lowest node ID. Here "E" has no edges, so it joins the first set even though it is conceptually unrelated to "A" and "C": ::: {#c3c5848f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("C", "D")]) ) set_a, set_b = graph.bipartite_sets() ( [graph.get_label_from_id(i) for i in set_a], [graph.get_label_from_id(i) for i in set_b], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (['A', 'C', 'E'], ['B', 'D']) ``` ::: ::: A triangle can't be split into two sides, so the method raises a `ValueError`: ::: {#af34a6af .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} triangle = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(n=3) try: triangle.bipartite_sets() except ValueError as e: print(e) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Graph is not bipartite ``` ::: :::
